Extent: 110 folios; Subject: Tantra; Author: Śrī Mahāmaheśvarācārya.
Folio 1a) Oṃ. Homage to the lotus feet of the venerable Guru. Oṃ tat sat.

Oṃ. To the Supreme One, whose own sovereign power has blossomed within the manifestation of the non-manifest, who delights in the supreme abode of play which is the body of supreme bliss, [to] His own Lord...

Victory to that Great Soul, known as Śiva, who is the supreme sky, whose heart is filled with the overflowing nectar of the Supreme arising from the strings [of the cosmic lute]. Now, here indeed is the Supreme Self, surging forth from unconditioned and infinite sovereignty.

The Supreme Lord, who consists of the light and bliss of the dyad, manifests His own majesty— which appears as the singular essence of the meaning of all scriptures— through His own power (*śakti*) that has attained identification with Him, in order to bring about the recognition of His own true nature.
Having first perceived [the sound] as *paśyantī* and then as *madhyamā*,

the independent Supreme Lord, through the state of *vaikharī*, makes it manifest; for in the absence of the differentiation of the reflective awareness of His own essential nature, there is no manifestation of anything else.

Pṛ0 2ba) Possessing by eternal union the power of action whose nature is sovereignty— consisting of differentiation and, once differentiated, non-differentiation through internal synthesis— the Great Lord, whose essence is light and bliss, is self-established as the creator of the universe.
The empire of His own nature, which is devoid of objective appearance, unfolds by His own will from His essential self;

for, possessing attributes such as fullness, eternity, and pervasiveness, the majesty of His own powers has blossomed forth. As it is said: "In whom all is, and from whom [all proceeds]... (Yasmin sarvam).

Salutations to Him who is everything, who is from everything, who is everything, and who is eternally composed of everything— to that Self of all, whose essential nature is animated by sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*),
and who [possesses] the five primary powers (*pañcaśakti*) as His own manifestation.
That [Self], having transcended the state of being composed of dogs, causes one to experience the wonder of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of play;

and it has been said by the Great Teachers: "From the desireless and full [Self], that which previously manifested as the 'I' subsequently projects the branches [of the world] when there is expectation."

I bow to that non-dual totality which consists of the supreme Śiva and Śakti— the light-form, the perfectly full, resting within its own self— which, though divided from its essential nature into its own constituent parts, partakes in the states of expansion, manifestation, withdrawal, and persistence.
I bow to that which is the entire universe.

Thus, it is filled with the great bliss of Tiṃta and saturated by the rays of the consciousness of will (*icchā-saṃvit*); it is completely full of infinite power (*ananta-śakti*). Furthermore, the Root Nature (*mūla-prakṛti*) is that which takes the form of the transformation of His will and serves as the cause for the emergence of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), the individual body (*piṇḍa*), and so forth; it is the transformation thereof.

It is said that the nature of the Supreme Lord is sung as being characterized by the essence of manifold variety; thus: "Beyond the modification [of Prakṛti] is Mahat, and from that, Ahaṃkāra. Even though there is the diversity of creation within those modifications, the Supreme is distinct from them.
The Puruṣa, because his nature is eternally existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), shines forth with supreme luminosity; because he is of the nature of light and is uniquely eternal,
this Lord never undergoes the inevitable modifications [of material existence].

Having produced the diversity of emission from primordial nature (prakṛti) through observation, and having brought about the states of agency and non-agency, he— acting as a witness to those operations—
describes agency and non-agency by way of their ultimate limit.
Like a jewel or the sun, the Great Lord (Maheśa), whose singular body is the light of consciousness,

is by nature the witness of that [universe] which, though impelled by some force of effort toward the emergence of Māyā, manifests as the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of the unfolding of Māyā.

Thus, since the agency of *prakṛti* and the non-agency of *puruṣa* are proclaimed by all [authorities] as being established by their very nature— like the sun and the sun-crystal— all specific living beings are portions and sub-portions of these two. This much is the intent regarding their origin.
By the word "mātra" (only), the nature of the Supreme Lord, which is filled with its own inherent wonder, has essentially been shown.
Now, one might ask: why is the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a constituent part of those two, the opposite of that? To this he says: "the contracted person" (*saṃkucita-puruṣa*).
The meaning of the verse is as follows: the remainder [of the phrase] is "due to being overcome by delusion" (*mohābhibhavāt*).

For the conscious aspect (*cidaṃśa*), when it revolves with great velocity, conceives—as if through a delusion—that its own inherent portion of *prakṛti*, which serves as its substrate, is identical to itself, and thus attains identity with that [unconscious matter].
Thus, even Mahāvīra— whose human effort was contracted, who had forgotten his own innate sovereignty, and whose power was dependent on the expansion of *prakṛti*—
appears as if diminished; he clarifies this very point by stating that the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) is essentially of the nature of expansion.
Due to the conceit of identity between the object of knowledge and the knower, the manifestation of his own power becomes contracted;
deluded by *māyā*, fallen from his own nature through the gateway of the internal and external organs, he attains an outward expansion [and thus] loses the supreme crest of consciousness.

"From that, the Self-born [Lord] cut [the bonds]; therefore, they do not perceive the Supreme within themselves"— by this Śruti it is shown that one who has bound oneself with the cords of attachment, being overwhelmed by the vision of modification (vikāra-dṛṣṭi),
falls into servitude to dharma and adharma and transmigrates through various wombs.

(p. 8b) Transmigration, indeed, consists merely of the conceptualization of delusion; in reality, there is no loss of its own nature whatsoever. For transmigration has dependence as its cause and consists of the modifications of primordial matter (*prakṛti*); thus, that very [nature] is now being examined.

The modification (*vikṛti*) produced from the primary nature (*prakṛti*)—which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) that have attained transformation through the three powers—is twofold, distinguished as individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*).
That [primary nature] is of two kinds according to its gross, subtle, and pervasive operations; it is the material cause (*upādāna*) and the veil (*āvaraṇa*).

The five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtāni*), which consist of the gradations of the transformations of that subtle essence of existence, pervade the gross and subtle limbs; thus, the Puruṣa exists within them in various forms as their witness (*sākṣitvena*). (Page 9b)

Through the vibration of that [principle] which has attained activity, the heart, abdomen, and other organs proceed to their respective functions; due to the conjunction of diverse states, there arises the nature of fluctuation in the form of the perishable,
consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) in the form of gross phlegm, bile, wind, and blood.
(p. 10a) Due to the non-differentiation of the *ratas*, at every single point within the infinite varieties of what are called creation and dissolution,
the gatekeepers— whose forms consist of the power of their respective locations and who are interwoven with the mechanism of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— attain union, just as at the time of creation.
At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the seven constellations (*nakṣatras*)— beginning with Aries at its first degree and ending with Pisces at its last degree—
are joined together with one another. During the period of the stability of the cycle of creation (*sṛṣṭi-kāla-sthiti-avasara*),
their internal conjunctions and the specific states dependent upon them are likewise set forth.

Just as, through the mutual conjunction of the planets, there arise the Kṛta and other ages due to the predominance of auspicious or inauspicious strength— wherein the dissolution known as Antakoṭi occurs,
and having abandoned here itself the transformation of bone and flesh acquired [in previous lives]— [there remains only] the auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Relying upon this, it shines forth in the form of another source; just as the five great elements, which are transformations of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) resulting from the conjunction of the *tamas* portion,
shine forth in another form after relinquishing their final manifestation, so too is its momentum.

O Lord, at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), all beings are submerged like blades of grass by the surging waters of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); having brought each thing back to its own cause and thereby effecting their complete dissolution therein, [the Lord remains] in His pure essential nature.

The Supreme Lord remains as the syllable *Mahāvyoma* (the Great Void); thus, he shows that even for one who is fit [for liberation], it occurs through the contemplation of one's own true nature alone. From the realization of that—[which is] the state of liberation consisting of a true knowledge of one's own nature, devoid of all conceptualization of divisions—[liberation arises].
Liberation is not of the nature of the direct realization of one's own power and sovereignty;

rather, it is perfect knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), which consists in the true knowledge of one’s own self— which is of the nature of reality, consciousness, and bliss— as being identical in essence with the Supreme Self, the innermost mind, as it truly is.
It is not the reality consisting of the conceptualization of forms such as recitation, meditation, and so forth; rather,
it is that which arises from supreme consciousness through the realization of the identity of the word and its meaning—
a state free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), in which the appearance of the entire manifold world has been stilled, and which is one's own true self.

The supreme space shines forth with absolute excellence; however, O Hero, it is said that liberation comes from knowledge alone and not otherwise. For among all other means, awakening is the direct and singular means to liberation, just as fire is to the cooking of food.

Furthermore, it is said that liberation is not accomplished without the knowledge of reality (*vajñjñāna*). Since the nature of that very knowledge is the self-manifestation of the Self, that knowledge itself is liberation; it is not a going anywhere else.
Thus, knowledge and liberation have one and the same nature, as it has been said: "Liberation is not... (p. 13b).
Furthermore, [one might argue] that another name for it is simply the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa-prathana*), and that this nature of the self is consciousness (*saṃvit*).
But then, being carried away by the whirlpool of the force of *prakṛti*, how and where could one reconnect with one's own true nature? That which is directly...
Having spoken thus with the syllable *t-kāra*, he remains independent; therefore, it is said that at the end of that [syllable],

through the cessation of expansion (*unmeṣa*), one abides in the very nature of the fourth state (*turya*), which is the essence of non-conceptualization and the natural clarity of primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

Thus, as it was said: "I worship that which is the supreme, great void, devoid of divisions, full, consisting of Śiva and His Power, and which is the support for millions of Jīvas and Īśvaras shimmering with light that blazes upward and downward. (Folio 14b)
For this reason, by means of the logic of establishing one's own power at the initial and final limits,

having extracted one’s own Self— which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss— from the vast expansion [of the world] into the great ocean of one’s own consciousness, one should bring it to a state of equality with that fruit.

As it is stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "That state which arises at the end of waking and the beginning of sleep—one who contemplates that state directly attains imperishable bliss. Also in the *Vijñānabhairava*: "The prāṇa moves upward, for it moves downward... [p. 15b]... [fragmentary].

The individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is emission, moves as another; by supporting the two points of origin, it remains full through its state of sustenance. Through the turning back of the pair of spaces—whether internal or external—the *Bhairavī* [attains] the state of *Bhairava* in this manner.
The body is manifested in hunger and other states, at the beginning and end, in fear, in grief, in a cave,
in restraint, in haste, in curiosity, in hunger and other states, at the beginning and end, and in proximity to the reality of Brahman (*brahmasattā*).
In such ways, throughout all beginnings and ends, one should contemplate one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).

The realization must be performed because, through the vibration of one's own power manifested by the state of being oriented toward consciousness, sovereignty—which is the very nature of qualities such as omniscience—arises spontaneously from all states of existence. (p. 16b) Sovereignty is [thus] self-evident.

Just as the body yawns upon the emergence of memory, so too does it move through the capacity of the group of organs, such as the neck ornaments; that [capacity] is life, and its destruction is death—what indeed is it called? (p. 17a)
Anticipating the objection, "How could anything remain apart from these two, such that one might recognize [it]?", he says: "Transparency is the life of the sphere;
purity is the capacity for receiving the reflection of consciousness—this is the living soul."

(p. 17b) Through that [activity], when each respective state and its corresponding function manifest, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*) vibrates, having as its essential nature the transferral of the shadow of consciousness (*cicchāyā*). It is precisely from this vibration of the power of breath that the insentient body moves.
Just as iron becomes black with rust through contact with a magnet, so too, for those who are the foremost within their respective classes (as stated on page 18a),
there is a decline in such capacity;
this refers to the "lustre" (*chavi*), which consists in the inability to grasp the reflection of consciousness (*cid-chāyā*).
Only the body remains, devoid of duality and insentience, as the momentum of *prārabdha* karma is exhausted.
This alone constitutes the transformation of the physical aggregate (*piṇḍa-vikāra*), which consists of life and death; as it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "Though all-pervading... (p. 18b).

Due to the sealing of contraction fashioned by its own will, and under the influence of the flood of karma that yields various fruits, it assumes this or that body; impelled by the conscious self within this bodily machine— which is as firm as the wind-element— it wanders about.

Like a bellows or a leather bag filled with air, when the karma that impels them is exhausted, the mechanism of the body functions differently; the mechanism of the vital breath disintegrates and the body becomes like a wall.
Thus, the supreme subject is indestructible.
The inner self (pratyagātman), which is the witness of those two, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda),

and which is celebrated in all the Upaniṣads, is— through positive and negative concomitance— devoid of birth and death, distinct from the sheaths beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya), and is followed by all.

"Being the witness, the consenter, the supporter, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord, the Supreme Self—thus is the Supreme Person described within this body. By this statement, it is established that there is a supreme cognizer who is imperishable; for [the body] is not [the cognizer].
Just as there is no loss [of space] upon the destruction of a jar,
like the space situated within and without jars being devoid of that limiting adjunct (upādhi), so too the cognizer (pramātṛ) is devoid of that adjunct within the bodies.
[Page 20b] Its nature is that of consciousness (*saṃvit*), it is the vitalizing breath of all, the illuminator of all;
for it is the sun of consciousness (*saṃvinmārtāṇḍa*), the light of everything,
the unifying life-force of all appearances and names— the sun of consciousness.

By the power of manifesting all things, it illuminates the entire collection of existents; for indeed, without entering into the light of supreme consciousness, the self-nature of anything whatsoever cannot be established— whatever this may be.
Whatever appears, whether external to consciousness or internal, that very thing is the ground of its manifestation.
As it was said by the Great Gurus: "The faculty of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is the illuminator of the multitude of objects submerged within the great cave. (Mahāpṛ., fol. 21b)
How can we praise Śiva as "the one who is always present like a lamp in the heart"?

For it is thus: that power of radiance (*bharga-śakti*) of the Sun, which is the self of all reflections, illumines within its own consciousness the entire collection of manifested objects reflected therein.
It is reflected in all objects; though it is one,
it appears in manifold forms, just as space [appears] in jars,
or as the light of the sun appears in various forms according to whether the surfaces are clear or unclear.

The power of the Lord, whose nature is the capacity to manifest even within a sleeping jar— if that very same consciousness (cit) which adorns the vast expanse of the sky of consciousness resides in the sun, while that same consciousness resides in the belly of an insect dwelling within a hole in the earth; [it is one and the same].

Having been told that [the nature of the Self] is thus of one form, one might ask: "Why then are human beings distinguished from animals and the like by means of attaining identity with the Supreme Lord?
Anticipating this question, he says: "Because of the instruction on the withdrawal of the beginning and the end, up to the earth. (p. 23a)

In order to discern the difference in the nature of all things— from stones and the like up to human beings— by means of the gradations of expansion [of consciousness] against their contraction and insentient intent,
Maheśvara is indeed established as the primordial source; he is the one whose essential nature consists in the attenuation of insentience.
The human body is like a bee and a worm; it is the vessel for the illumination of the light of the Primordial God (Ādideva).
Its essence culminates in the *bindu*, and the secret instruction consists precisely in the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) of the letters *A* and *Ha*.

Just as another [entity] differs from the wealthy and the pure, so too—due to the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—there arises that which is like a sprout, possessing a swelling nature, dominated by *sattva*, and serving as the locus for the illumination of perception (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*). (p. 24a)
That which consists of their own essential nature, having attained existence through the internal and external senses and so forth,

is the perception of one's own Self as consciousness (*saṃvid-ātmaka*). Due to its nature of being submerged and emergent within that intended object, it possesses the distinction of being pure or impure.

Regarding what was stated concerning the remaining two types of souls—the Īśvara and the Anu—it is said that by bringing Māyā under his control, the Lord (Īśvara) becomes omniscient; however, the other [the Anu] remains subject to ignorance (avidyā), and due to the diversity of that [ignorance], he is manifold. This is the manifestation of the power of vision and action belonging to the Lord.
pṭ. 25a) Due to the simultaneous occurrence of both [states], there is a reversal for the person;
even in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is the loss of autonomy, and because of the lack of autonomy, there is non-cognition—thus the impurity of the individual soul (*āṇavamala*) is twofold.
By the word "man" (*nara*), there is the exclusion of the nature of [lower] beings;
[it refers to] those distinguished by the human species, such as humans, animals, and so forth, whose own nature consists of the various gradations of *rajas* and *tamas*. (Folio 25b)

Regarding that which was stated concerning the "obtainment": when illumination arises through all the gates in this body, that is knowledge; but when [ignorance] prevails, there is delusion, as well as greed, activity, and the undertaking of various actions. (Page 26a)
"O joy of the Kurus, when rajas increases, these arise: longing for the objects of desire, lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and delusion.
O bull of the Bharatas, when tamas increases, these arise: lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and delusion. Thus spoke the Lord.
He alone, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the like, possessed of all sovereignty,
is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), the vitalizer of all, the knower of all, and the witness of all— because his own nature is not an object for anyone— he [perceives] himself.
In the state of the gross elements (garu), forms (rūpa), and objects of sense (iṣubhāva), there is the knowledge and action that arise in response;

these three indeed constitute the nature of the bound soul (paśu). Through the persistence of sattva, rajas, and tamas, the individual soul (jīva), though full of these qualities, remains contracted. Thus, even while being complete, it is incomplete.
He shines forth through the recognition of his own true nature, endowed with qualities such as omniscience; they describe him as being of that very form.

By entering [into that state], one becomes identical with it; at the time of the practice of entering the fourth abode (*turya-dhāman*), which is one's own nature emerged from its own essence, one turns away from everything like the entry into the heart,
and thus the power [of consciousness] surges forth, possessing the perfection of vision and action.

By casting off the poverty of contraction through the power of *lāsya*, one attains the sovereignty of one's own consciousness; just as a worm, by means of its nature of turning away from all sides, [attains] the qualities of a bee that were previously contracted within itself— such is the meditation on that.

Just as [a lotus] becomes that very form by not expanding through entry [into water], likewise the individual soul (*jīva*) also— by the power of the contemplation "I am Śiva," which consists in the surrender of its own identity— has its innate power expanded.
Vaibhava is the state of attaining identity with the Supreme Lord; when,
through entry into the central abode, one remains as one with That, then, even while remaining in the body, one is devoid of division and free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

It abides as the very nature of space; how and where can that reality, whose own-nature is characterized by the distinctions of pure and impure, be perceived within the moon, sun, and fire, [remaining] as it is without obscuration?
The Lord, the God who is free from disease and whose essential nature is immutable, having descended from his own form—
which consists of the equilibrium of bliss and consciousness— as the twelve-fold solar manifestation known as the venerable Anāhata-Bhaṭṭāraka, [manifested] his own power...

Just as [the sun] manifests its own light within the wall-like substrate that is the aggregate of the unmanifested and the manifested, so too, through the manifestation of the stability of the rain of the collective aggregate of the self when it is unobscured, there occurs the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between Soma and Agni.
By those two [powers], there is the pervasive [consciousness] consisting of five powers, which is the inherent substratum of the five [elements],

the illuminator of the functions [of the senses], and endowed with twelve digits (kalās); according to the principle stated in such passages as "the primordial consciousness is transformed into prāṇa," it is the pervader of both the general and the particular.

[Page 30b] She causes the descent of the thousand rays, which are of the nature of Parā, to arise in the space of Mūlaprakṛti; having established her station in the locus of these three abodes, she is Parāśakti—thus he says that very thing: "Her own self is Śakti."
This supreme Śakti, having embraced the multitude of sounds (śabdarāśi),

leads her own self into the state of Kuṇḍalinī— which consists of the three and a half coils of the Para, Parāpara, and Apara levels— and through the activity of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, [she manifests] the entire [universe].
It proliferates manifold conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) due to its crookedness; thus,
with a mental state that flows in a devious manner and having forgotten its own self-awareness through that lack of autonomy,
it becomes a partaker in the experience of the fruits consisting of auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

All living beings have fallen into distress; he states the method for removing that distress: "In the union [of the three], when one contemplates the subject (pramātṛ), supreme accomplishment is attained. One should meditate there upon the union of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
"O Dear One, by the yoga of churning the middle [channel], straightness arises; according to this principle,
through the union of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, one becomes filled with the intensity of one's own supreme love, and [attains] the middle..."
Having realized one's own self as the substrate through the method of churning the *āsava*,

and having brought that [self] to a state of straightness by means of the disappearance of its curved form, one meditates on the upward movement resulting from the entry into the supreme *nāda*. From this upward movement...
It causes the arousal of the *mānadaṇḍa* (the staff of pride), which consists of the mutual friction [of the two],
having entered that state of absorption (*madhyapadavī*) unknown to both Light (*prakāśa*) and Bliss (*ānanda*), namely this pair known as the Sun and the Moon.
Swallowing and entering upward, the individual soul— whose lineage has been reduced to ashes by the fire of the resonance (nāda)— enters the unmanifest Śiva through negligence;
this is indeed the union of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Having accomplished what is desired, she arises like Īśvara as the essence of great power (*mahāvīryātmikā*).
By means of these three powers, she performs the general acts of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal— beginning with the gross and the subtle— which fall within the range of ordinary perception.

Just as the moon waxes and wanes through the bright and dark fortnights of the seasons, so too, when that [Supreme] merges with the assembly [of energies], He—having contemplated His own Self as Truth and Knowledge with equanimity—performs creation and the other cosmic acts, like the emanation of a mental resolve.
