When consciousness enters this supreme state (*piparamepadeśa*) through the continuous contemplation of the light of consciousness,
all actions become means for entering the supreme abode.
Thus, these states— beginning with waking, dreaming, and ending with deep sleep and swoon— are indeed the three states that constitute *Śakti*.

The threefold triad of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna* is to be touched for the sake of igniting the light of the fourth state. Having thus indicated [the means], he states another method for entering the supreme reality (*paratattva*). [He says: "contraction... (*saṃkoca*)...

By means of the two [powers] of expansion and contraction, through the power of observing self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), one brings about the simultaneous emergence and cessation of the functions of the internal and external organs; thus,
one is empowered by people as the sovereign lord of the wheel of one's own powers (*svaśakticakreśatva*).
A certain hero necessarily attains the inner Self, as stated in another Vedic scripture: "He who has turned his gaze away [from the external] and beholds the inner Self enjoys immortality.
Thus, like the contraction of a tortoise's limbs, the functions of all the internal and external organs are simultaneously withdrawn.
Regarding that which was stated in the *Gītā* concerning withdrawal:

"When one withdraws these senses from the objects of the senses in every way, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom is firmly established" (Gītā 2.58). Even during the occasion of outward expansion, his own [mind] remains [withdrawn].

Regarding what was said about their respective objects being established through the power of the mind— "having cast all powers, beginning with perception, simultaneously upon each of their own objects,
remain in the middle like a pillar of gold"— [that is now explained].
On page 36b), he states another perspective:

"The unification with the Great Purpose" (*mahārthasaṃdhāna*) refers to the continuous realization of the nature of supreme consciousness (*paramārthasaṃvit*), which is all-pervasive and superior to all objects, as the "I" (*aham*).

Self-awareness consisting of reflective discernment (*tyavamarśātmasaṃvedana*) must always be maintained with full attentiveness during all investigations of words and their meanings (p. 37a). Through the excellence of its cultivation, it serves to pacify all disturbances without exception and [removes] the stain of doubt.

One should enter the abode of the supreme state; however, for one who has not attained that state due to slow practice, all obstacles arise. Therefore, having become steady-minded through unimpeded effort, [one should enter] the supreme state.
One should abide in the state beyond exhaustion; furthermore,
this yoga is the emergence of existence from non-existence, wherein being appears as the semblance of truth,
and which consists of the nature of the arousal and stabilization of existence— this is the upward surge of power (*śaktyudgama*).
The nature of non-emission (*acyutasvabhāva*) is the means for entering into the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Through the firm state of identity with that,
one establishes a natural stability within one's own self— which is of an unemitted nature—
at every moment, as if in a moment characterized by both dissolution and emergence.

In specific states, one does not deviate from one's true nature; indeed, effort is exerted through well-being. (Page 38b) Having analytically determined those activities conducive to well-being as being free from agitation, the one who is healthy [perceives] the activities of mental affliction, such as attachment and recollection.

When subtle diseases have arisen, one who is skilled in their medical treatment should attend to them while remaining healthy. For just as attachment arises in a man who contemplates poisons, from that attachment desire is born.
From desire arises anger; from anger arises delusion;
delusion is the confusion of memory; from the loss of memory comes the destruction of the intellect; and from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes.
Thus, it is solely through attachment to defects such as desire and anger that this occurs.
They arise through the cultivation of attachment to those who are not disciples; one should pacify all of them.
If they arise from procreation, their opposites, such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, must be sought as their remedies. This is the secret perspective.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the great disease; through its lack of autonomy, it is like the possession by the five great elements. Therefore, all things designated as "elements" move about as delusions and intoxications.
For the sake of pacifying that, [one should realize] the light and bliss within oneself.

By the word "without effort," he remains established as one who is self-abiding (*svastha*). For one who is always attentive, dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the like follow him like servants. However, when the mind—which consists of the five breaths—is powerful and intent upon sustaining [the body], anger and the other [afflictions] arise.
By what power of reasoning do they proceed under control, and how does one bring them to pacification?

To this he says: "Discrimination (*vitarka*) is the supreme medicine," for it is the cause of the nourishment of discernment (*viveka*) and contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and thus it eliminates all afflictions (*āyāsa*).

The *sakara* is the supreme medicine; by its grace, yogins abandon the weakness consisting of the contraction of their own self and, having attained supreme heroism, shine forth like a mass of blossoming lotuses. Thus it is said:
"Not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
Having distinguished between the existent and non-existent through reasoning, having pacified the adversaries of the Dharma,
and having brought all the faculties to a state of clarity through the serenity of one’s own intrinsic awareness, one then attains the qualities [of the path].

Coexistence with pride (*māna*) is of two kinds: [the former] is indifference toward the engagement and withdrawal of the qualities (*guṇas*), as stated by the Blessed One: "O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they have fully set in. (Gītā 14.22) [The latter is] the absence of such indifference.
Free from longing and not turning back, he sits like one indifferent, unshaken by the *guṇas*.
"The *guṇas* alone revolve"—thus perceiving, he neither stands nor moves;
equal in pain and pleasure, established in himself, he is the same amidst the *guṇas*.

One who is equal toward stone and gold, to whom the pleasant and unpleasant are alike, who is steadfast, for whom censure and self-praise are the same, who is the same in honor and dishonor, who is the same toward the parties of friend and foe, and who has renounced all undertakings— that person has transcended the qualities.

Thinking, "These qualities, though existing as the attributes of the aggregate, are not capable of agitating me," he does not deviate from his own true nature; thus he becomes one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*). Second, by his own power, he possesses movement at will.

The production of motionlessness is a quality; for that which has transformed into the nature of inclination (*ruci*), that inclination consists of faith (*śraddhā*). Thus, this threefold operation is previously designated as *sāttvikī*, *rājasī*, and *tāmasī*. (Page 43b)
Through the distinctions of unfolding (*unmīlana*), closing (*nimīlana*), and simultaneous closing and unfolding (*avalīmīlana*), this [nature] is ninefold;

yet, through such divisions, it is of infinite varieties due to the predominance of each individual [aspect] and its connection with the functions (*vṛtti*) of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. For these are indeed the qualities (*guṇas*).

Having attained existence as the subject (*pramātṛ*), and having entered into one's own self-consciousness whose nature is the reflective awareness of "I" by relying on the power situated within that [subject], one manifests the appearance of the object and the subject at will, according to one's own desire.
Furthermore, that contemplation which consists of the thought, "I am Śiva— the unfragmented Self whose nature is perfect, independent bliss, whose body is the radiance of the universe,
and who is free from the three impurities"— that alone is the supreme medicine for one whose sovereignty is contracted.
Having dispelled the afflictions of birth, death, and the like for the liberated soul,
he reveals his own abiding state within the Self alone in the immortal abode known as Paramaśiva; for such a yogi is indeed one whose power has arisen.

The excellence of that very Self-power is this: that it effortlessly unfolds, within its own self, those successions of births—which serve as witnesses to one's deeds in this world and the next and which constitute the very fabric of existence—and simultaneously causes them to dissolve back into its own nature. This is its preeminence.
(p. 45b) Since the nature [of the witness] is submerged, it is like a witness to both this world and the next, just as in the states of dreaming and waking.

Here, since the subject (*pramātṛ*) is necessarily engaged in the well-functioning [mental] states, one must certainly accept its status as a witness; how could it not be so in the next world? Thus [the author] anticipates the objection.
What is this Heart-Light? Since it is the locus where the expansion and repose of all objective mental states (*dṛśya-vṛtti*) occur, it is the Light of Consciousness (*cit-prakāśa*);
therefore, by manifesting that [Light], it is reflected within the mirror of one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).
Having illuminated all classes of phenomena that have come here and there as reflections,
it is the witness of their activity, as stated in the *Vasiṣṭha* (in the section on the Bestowal of Self-Knowledge): "Within this expansive [consciousness],
all these various classes of objects..."

"The reflection [is like] a tree on the bank of a lake"— in such a state, through the withdrawal of both external and internal mental activity, there is a disregard for heedlessness (*pramāda*), and within that heedlessness, the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) is conceived.

(p. 47a) When there arises the reflection that even the expansion of supernatural powers (*siddhi-prapañca*), though white [pure], is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*)—because it lacks independence and because its own nature is empty—and that it must be rejected due to the force of the surging forth of one’s own innate magnanimity; when [this occurs]...
He perceives like a spider; then, through the dissolution of that creation, he becomes established in the Supreme Reality (p.

47b). [The opponent asks: "In such a manifold display of supernatural powers (siddhi), how can one effect their subordination? To this he says: "Satisfied," meaning when one is satiated by the various manifestations of sovereignty.

Through the attainment of that Self, which possesses the sovereignty of *hā* and the other [powers], and through the unification with one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), one becomes filled with joy; thus, all desires are uprooted, and that very state is capable of fulfilling every aspiration. (p. 48a) It is that indeed.
The supreme limit, adorned by the higher and lower [states], clarifies the coloring of objects that serve as the locus for distraction by means of the state of one-pointedness;
it is the movement of the tip of a hair on one's own body.

On page 48b): In the act of contemplation (*cintana*), there is the knowledge (*jñāna*) resting upon the primordial nature (*prakṛti*); its supreme limit is the surging state that transcends that [nature]. Having ascended to that [limit], one is freed from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects—whether gross or subtle, external or internal, pertaining to this world or the next.

The liberated Paramahaṃsa describes his state [as follows]: "The Paramahaṃsa is situated upon the lotus (padmāsana). Because it has a single opening and possesses the nature of simultaneous contraction and expansion, the wheel of powers (śakticakra) itself is the lotus."
The Paramahaṃsa, who effects creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace, abides as the Lord;
through the medium of his innate power (*nijā-śakti*), he is celebrated as the Great Sound (*mahārāva*) which transcends the *Ha* (the letter *ha*). That...
"The gods rejoice and live by taking refuge in his heart, which is Brahman.

Thus, the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) itself is his body. He describes the true nature of such a person established in the stage of the supreme ascetic (*paramahaṃsāśrama*) as being "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*).
O Soma, whatever shines— whether external or internal, illuminated by the sun, the moon, or fire— all that is within the range of the intellect; therein the sun does not shine,
nor the moon or the stars, nor do these lightnings shine, much less this fire.
Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this world is illumined.
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines That;
it is my supreme abode, having gone to which they do not return. By its persistence—

Having transcended [all things] through the singular convergence of all powers, that state of rest— which is free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*), radiant with the expansion of its own innate luster, and whose nature is independent—
is the innate nature (*sahaja-svabhāva*) of that Sovereign Self. For one who has ascended to that station, there is no outward-going [of the mind].
On the occasion of the *gamādi* [the movement of breath], he speaks of the one situated within the world:

"The state of existing in a nature manifested by one's own autonomy (*svātantrya*)—that is the 'unfettered' (*nirgalā*) [state]. I alone am the supreme cause, the Swan (*haṃsa*), the Auspicious One (*śiva*)."

Abiding [in this state], the reflective awareness of "I," whose nature is everywhere unimpeded, performs worldly transactions as it desires— preceded by either crookedness or straightforwardness— and characterized by the conceptual constructions beginning with rejection and acceptance and ending with pride.
As it has been said: "In some places excellent, in some fallen, in some like spirits and *piśācas*, the yogi wanders upon the surface of the earth assuming various guises"—
such is the nature of one who exists in the ten stages (*daśāvṛtta*).

He describes the state of stability: "Reeling" means that, intoxicated by the conversation of unsurpassed bliss, one has flooded the wheel of the internal and external senses with its fullness; thus, through the mode of half-closing [the eyes], all activity reels like one intoxicated by wine. (p. 52b)

This is directly indicated by what is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha*: "Though remaining inward-turned and even engaged in external activity, one appears as if constantly sleepy due to being utterly exhausted.
Now, in the supreme state, there is no distinction between external and internal activity...
(p. 53a) Thus, in the state of tranquility, the wonder of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) shines forth;
however, during its expansion, one necessarily experiences the fruition of past actions (*prārabdha-bhoga*).
Anticipating the question, "How is such a nature of reality (*svabhāva-tattva*) to be accepted?", he says: *amā-pūrṇā*.
And that power of theirs, whose form is nectar and whose nature is external radiance,
having satisfied the gods and the ancestors by resting in the Supreme Subject,
remains as wonder; that very [power] is the state of the Supreme Subject.
From the two [doors] up to the limit of the *ullāsa*, that which possesses the power to manifest and nourish all things— whose nature is ever-present and undeniable—
is this very glory of mine, like the fierce sun; thus [he perceives it] directly.
The Lord of Yogins shines as one whose own nature has been accomplished; for him, there is nothing whatsoever apart from the manifestation of his own essential form.
Bhairava, the Lord of Yogins, describes the majesty of such a yogin as follows:

The power of the Supreme Lord (Anuttarādideva), which consists of the manifestation of all vital breaths, forms, and activities, has been transformed by Time; it impels the various diversities of modifications, which are of the nature of the unfolding of primordial matter (prakṛti), as they are woven within itself. Time [is that which impels].

Indeed, because it possesses both internal and external natures, it revolves the wheel of the seven *ṛkṣas* (constellations) by means of two paths— the southern and the northern— and through that revolution, it manifests the division of the decrease and increase of day and night by means of units such as *truṭis*, *muhūrtas*, and so forth.

He encompasses all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); all living beings, from the gods down to the stationary, are dependent upon Him; He is the devourer of all, the glorious Lord Mahābhairava, who arises as the playful manifestation of the wealth of both the non-manifest and the manifest.
The Lord of Yogins, who is independent and filled with wonder and amazement, is by nature untainted by rising or setting; for he is everywhere full of his own wondrous splendor,
[residing] in the hearts of those devoted worshippers who have become one with his own self.

May the Great Lord, who directly realizes the nature of his own sovereign power, be gracious. Thus ends [the section on] the Supreme Lord in the *Svātantryadīpikā*, composed by the eminent teacher, the great Maheśvara.

The First Chapter (Prathamollāsa), titled "The Exposition of the Means for Attaining Absorption into that [Reality] which is Vast in its Manifestations," page 56b. Oṃ! To the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose essential nature is light and bliss, there is but one supreme power (Parāśakti) which constitutes his very own nature.
That very [consciousness] manifests as the self of all; though one, it appears in manifold forms.

For all these beings are its parts. (Gītā 15.7) "In this world of living beings, I am the eternal soul that has become the life-force within all creatures. [And: "The senses, with the mind as the sixth... (Gītā 15.8)

That which, by its very nature, abides in proximity [to consciousness], yet— though possessing that same essence— is turned away from it; thereby having attained the state of a bound soul (paśu), its nature becomes dependent upon the internal and external organs,
which consist in the contraction of its own power.
Page 57b) Furthermore, outward-oriented superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is precisely that state of being a bound animal (*paśutva*) and a state of partiality;
for one who is turned away from the Supreme Lord who is his own self, and who is impoverished of power,
there is the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) consisting of the blossoming of his own inherent power.

First, in order to establish [the foundation], the supreme power of the Lord, Parā Kālī, who is the heart of the Supreme Lord and whose essential nature is expanded as the self of each and every infinite world,
is described at length as the source of all powers.

The Lord Maheśvara is the locus of the expansion and repose of the powers (śakti). He is the Supreme Sovereign Lady (Bhaṭṭārikā), who is the essence of the five powers that constitute the eternal Yoginīs, whose nature is the vitalizing breath of supreme freedom, and who is the Unsurpassed (Anuttara).

This [reality], having attained a vibration of delight through the acquisition of affection, flashes forth in the form of will, knowledge, and action; and with the desire to project itself outward as "this," it assumes those three forms which arrest its own essential nature.
Having manifested as *prakṛti*— which is of the nature of obstruction, characterized by "this-ness" (*idantā*), designated as *māyā*,
and consisting primarily of contraction in the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—
and which is essentially the power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*) possessing the nature of the seed and the womb; (pṛ0 59a) ...the seed-nature...
Having said, "Do not abandon me, O son," he created two lineages known as Nara and Īśa, who were his own portions;

by the opening and closing of his sovereignty, he manifested them in single and multiple forms within those various specific locations characterized by the swelling of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (Page 59b)
It shines appropriately with the rays of its blossoming voice;

those rays consist of the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire. Through them—whose essential forms are expansion, maintenance, and withdrawal—all this [universe] is made to be of the nature of "That" (Tadātman).
She establishes [the universe] and devours it; thus, as Kālī whose nature consists of twelve aspects, having performed the play of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal,
she is the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*) because all doubts and residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been completely stilled within her own essential nature.
(Page 60b) "She attains exhaustion"—thus, the Supreme Power of the Lord (Pārameśvarī) alone shines everywhere.
To show that there is no one whatsoever who can cause agitation in her while she accomplishes such a variety of actions, he says: "Unagitated, [she is] the self-luminous..."

When this agency— which is pervaded by the nature of being a knower within the self— and which has been expanded into the grand display of the universe, is [realized] as having the essential nature of unimpeded light and bliss,
it is everywhere independent, consisting of memory, knowledge, and the removal of ignorance.
Though she is capable in the various functions of those respective states and, while resting in other subjects as it were, pervades the universe, she is nonetheless transcendent;

she is the self-existent reality within the hearts of all, and her essential nature is as follows: [Page 61b] She is that very [consciousness] which, though appearing as the various states of the limited subject, remains established in the Supreme Subject; though she manifests the universe, she is beyond it; she is the Self residing in the hearts of all beings, and therein lies her true nature.
To determine this, he says: "By virtue of her skill, she is the impeller within all living beings;
she is consciousness itself, the producer of all knowledge in all entities, possessing all arts, and by virtue of her skill, she is the nature of both the pervaded and the pervader."

There, in the seat (pīṭha) at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], she whose nature is the treasury of knowledge resides in the heart as the life-function; likewise, through the expansion of the thread known as the "end of the twelve," like a magician, she manifests both internally and externally.

By transferring the operations of knowledge and action into these [senses], it manifests an illusion (*māyā*) whose nature is their activity; and like a blacksmith, through the impelling of the machine of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it inflames Vaiśvānara situated in the stomach, which resides within the heart.
Having extracted [the essence] through the discernment of the essential and the non-essential, he cooks the food and drink;

from that, the essence is led to the place of the liver (*yakṛt*). There too, having again distinguished between the essential and the non-essential, it takes on the nature of the various powers (*śakti*) whose form is the manifestation of his own rays of light.

It draws forth the essence of each [element] from its respective place as appropriate; by making the lunar digit (*somakalā*) powerful, it nourishes all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). In that regard, there is the bringing about of depletion, restoration, immobilization, and equilibrium.

(63b) Shining with the five powers whose nature is the non-pervasive substratum, vitality itself consists of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of Soma and Agni; it has made its abode in the midst of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni.
"Having the nature of the thirty-six *kalās*," and so forth; thus, from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the lower opening, consciousness alone is omnipresent.
Those who turn away from it are "bound souls" (*paśu*). He states this very point: "Due to its aversion, the individual soul (*jīva*) is dependent on another."
According to the principle stated in the passage, "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings," the Supreme Consciousness itself has become the Self within the hearts of all;
yet, due to its dual orientation, it is contracted in nature, characterized by the forgetting of its own true essence.

The manifestation of its own power, having attained identity with *prakṛti*, transforms into the form of consciousness as the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the *prāṇa* and the mind (*cetas*) are mutually connected, and the various specific states of consciousness are of the nature of the modifications (*vṛtti*) of those two.

In locations such as the heart and the rest, the soul—expanding almost to its full extent and assuming a state of identity with the respective natures of those places—follows the qualities (*guṇas*) and remains situated there like the relationship between milk and clarified butter; thus, it is dependent upon them. Tattaccha... [text fragment]
Due to the delusion caused by the wheel of the *mātṛkā* (phonemes), whose nature is the vibration of the void, his knowledge is colored by external manifestations;
overcome by false cognitions and by desire, anger, greed, pride, envy, sorrow, joy, and the like—(p. 65b).

Being overwhelmed by birth, death, and disease, one is defeated; as it has been said: "Established in *sattva*, established in *rajas*, and established in *tamas*, the experiencer of the qualities wanders in this manner, O Goddess, going from one state to another" (p. 66a). Thus he travels.

"Residing in the center of the consciousness of the apertures, hanging down from the noose of Brahmā, the Sovereigns of the Pīṭhas repeatedly delude [beings] with the Great Terrible One"— thus, by means of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) consisting of mind, ego, and intellect, which takes the form of the emergence of those [subtle] elements.
pṛ0 66ba) "Restrained, [one perceives] the arising of cognitions produced from that" (Yoga Sūtra 1.32).

For one who has reached such a state, he describes the means for removing afflictions, which consists in the cessation of delusion: "the observation of the instability of the body, [and its origin in] semen and blood."

One should contemplate the instability of the body— which is imagined, subject to the six transformations, and afflicted by the ten defects— by reflecting upon it as being like bubbles arising from the current of a river. [Sukha...]

Perceiving that this wretched body is merely a receptacle for sufferings and is as fragile as a bubble, one observes that its relatives, such as family members and the like, are likewise subject to that same fate;
thus [the realization becomes] intense.

For one who has attained firmness in the cultivation of detachment from worldly objects, he states the cause for abiding in one's own Self, which consists of the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss: "Having renounced attachment...
for the sake of realizing That, one should approach a Guru... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).

Page 68a): According to the Śruti, "One should approach a learned Brahmin established in Brahman," one should go into the presence of those whose passion and hatred have dissolved and whose supreme awakening has blossomed,
and perform service, prostration, and so forth once again.

Having heard with one's heart and ears those words spoken with such devotion, one must act in accordance with them; for the observance of his command alone is the supreme merit, while departing from it is a great transgression.
Indeed, the company of virtuous ones who have ascended to the supreme reality is conducive to attaining the highest state, but not that of those devoid of true awakening who are merely talkative;
for one's own nature proceeds in accordance with the company one keeps. (Page 69a)
It is well said: those whose hearts have been purified by the experience of resting in the unsurpassed state through supreme association, being the most excellent of all,
are capable of rescuing others by means of the logic of the instructions of that tradition.
"By seeing or even by touching [this], the lords of yogins, established in the conduct of their lineage, will cause one to cross over the vast ocean of existence"—thus it has been said.
[This refers to] that which nourishes the abiding in one's own nature; having attained that...
He clarifies that reasoning (*yukti*) which consists of "contemplation of the middle" (*madhyacintanātmikā yuktiḥ*, p.

70a): within the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), such as its internal and external movement, contraction, expansion, and suspension, there is the surging forth of consciousness (*saṃvit*) consisting of contemplation of the middle.

The reasoning regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is the cause for the thorough knowledge of one's own self, which is the supreme consciousness whose essence consists of all substrates; just as fire arises from the friction of wood and clarified butter from the churning of milk, [it is distinct] in its specific character.

The sense is that, in the same way, through the practice of contemplating the "middle" (the state between existence and non-existence), the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of one's own self (*svātman*) will arise. Now, one might ask: since there are many obstacles that act as impediments to abiding in one's true nature (*svarūpasthiti*), how can those [obstacles] be overcome?

Regarding the statement "one should pacify," it is said: through the excellence of practice, there is the removal of obstacles; through the excellence of cultivating the intermediate meditation, by means of the restraint of the fluctuations of the mind from this and that [object], [the mind becomes] intermediate moment by moment.
Through the non-forgetting of contemplation, there is the complete pacification of all disturbances— gross and subtle— such as mental agonies (*ādhi*) and physical ailments (*vyādhi*).
For one whose disturbances have been pacified, self-realization arises from one-pointedness of mind, free from *laya* (dissolution).
Through the casting aside of distraction, laziness, and the manifestation of various petty supernatural powers (*kṣudrasiddhi*),

and by means of the nature of stability in the *āva* (the state of non-dual awareness)— which consists of the essence of disregarding such displays through one-pointedness of mind and uninterrupted, thought-free meditation— the perfection of contentment and other virtues is attained.

In the heart of one who possesses faith and devotion, there arises the awakening to the Self, which consists of the expansion of one's own true nature and the attainment of pure being (*sattva*). This is the fourth stage (*bhūmikā*), characterized by the pervasion of the Self; otherwise, it is the pervasion of Śiva.

If, according to the rule, one desires the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by Śiva, then— being filled with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the firmness of an excess of faith and devotion— one who wishes to attain the state of Śaiva dharma should, by means of that flavor, perform the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of identity with Him.
With his body completely filled by the essence of the taste of the cool and pure nectar of the Self,
just as the activity of fish occurs effortlessly within water,
so too does the activity of the intellect, mind, vital breath, and senses occur for yogis alone.

Activity consists of the emergence of the manifestation of the other; for one such as this who is engaged in yoga, through the excellence of the emergence of the manifestation of the other— which is the very nature of that [yoga]— and through vows and austerity, he becomes endowed with all sovereign powers and pervades both internally and externally.

That vow which consists of worship characterized by the great conceit of the firm conviction "I am indeed the Supreme Lord," that alone is austerity whose very nature is the eradication of all impurities; for one who practices such a vow and austerity, the power of the Lord—
A state of clarity (*prasannatā*) characterized by expansion manifests everywhere for him;

and his recitation (*japa*), which is without means (*anupāya*) due to its non-differentiation, becomes unimpeded in its non-conceptual nature because the outward flow of internal discursive thought has been withdrawn.

When one perceives that essential nature— the supreme vibration (*paramaspanda*) which is Śiva, the "I," and primarily the power of vision (*paśyantī vāk*)— then the recitation (*japa*) consisting of radiant manifestation arises; however, when the recitation consists of the pacification of the triad (*tripuṭī*), it shines forth within the heart.
Now, the supreme gain arises from the total offering of one's entire self— the offering of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the body (*puñja*), the mind (*māyā*),

and the state of being the subject (*pramātṛtva*)— which consists in the cessation of the distinction between internal and external conceptual constructions through the unification of all differences. This is the supreme [attainment] resulting from the complete surrender of everything.
The attainment of the Supreme Lord, who is a mass of light and bliss, is direct realization.
As it has been said: "When the fourfold—mind, consciousness, power, and the self—is dissolved into the Beloved, that is the body of Bhairava."
Page 75b) and so forth. This very *apūrṇāhuti*, consisting of the offering of everything without remainder,

awakens the fire of that [realization] which has arrived through the excellent path and which burns away the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of both auspicious and inauspicious actions accumulated over many lifetimes.

The Lord Caitanya is satisfied by the face [of the devotee], and being well-pleased with the state of devotion, He bestows the supreme perfection whose form is the great void (*mahāvyoma*). Thus it is said:
"From the arising of *udāna* comes the grace of *parā*, because of that equilibrium."

The capacity for upward movement (*pādanasāmarthya*) is the characteristic of *udāna* in all three [states] as appropriate; therefore, from that which has the nature of an intermediate force (*madhyabalasvarūpa*) arising from its activity,
there occurs the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of the Supreme Lord, whose essence is the abode of consciousness (*caitanyadhāmātmaka*).
The absorption into that self-nature is such that, as it is said, "Udāna is indeed the great fire," just as various specific substances cast into a fire are reduced to the state of the fire itself,
so too, through the arising of the function of Udāna, the vital breaths, the internal organs, and so forth [are absorbed].

By being offered as identical with that, they become truly one with knowledge (*jñāna*). It has been stated that through the submergence of the state of being vital breath (*prāṇa*) into *udāna*, there arises the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which is the power that follows after the vital breath and so forth.

The individual consciousness (*jīva-saṃvit*), which has become dependent upon states such as waking and so forth due to its departure from the refuge [of the Self], attains the fourth state (*turyā*)—
the nature of ultimate consciousness— from the emergence of the upward-grasping (*udādāna*) caused by the acquisition of its own innate power within the intermediate abode (*madhyadhāma*).

Having dissolved this entire universe, which consists of both difference and non-difference, into one's own self, she rests in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). As it is said [in the *Jagatkāya* on folio 78a]: "Having placed that [universe] within the Person, and from there within the heart, one perceives the Person situated in the Bindu."
And in that dense thicket called the "Dapiviya," this very thing known as knowledge—
which is likewise dense with supreme bliss and takes the form of the great void—
is victorious, for its nature is the experience of You; thus he speaks of those things characterized by ultimate rest.

The signs of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are horripilation and so forth; delusion (*bhrama*), trembling (*kampa*), and *pūrṇī*; and *plutā* and *ānanda*. These characteristics [occur] in sequence;
however, by skipping the sequence due to the intensity of bliss (*ānanda-prakarṣāt*), tears and horripilation manifest externally.

Regarding the attainment of that momentary absorption (*kṣaṇasamādhi*): when all mental fluctuations have subsided upon its manifestation, the absorption whose nature is self-luminous bliss is called *samādhi*.
Thus he describes its essential nature: "Through immersion, one becomes equal to the Lord by means of one's own consciousness. (p. 79a)
Through the method of self-contemplation, he has now awakened to the state of being worthy of gifts (*udānīyavṛtti*);

by the firmness of that [state], he has attained the nature of oneness with the Fourth (*turya*). By virtue of that oneness, even in states such as waking (*jāgrad-ādi*), his own sovereignty is manifested, and the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth have dissolved away. (p. 79b)

When one becomes fully absorbed in the abode of Rama-Shiva, through that absorption one shines forth like a sovereign emperor in all states of existence; even while living, one attains union with Shiva. As it has been said: "O, what a joy is the play of worldly happiness!"

(p. 80a) Liberation is difficult to attain; such good fortune exists on the path of liberation. O Śiva-yogins, when the Kali age has been broken, what could be more conducive to the practice of the *yāmala* (the union of Śiva and Śakti)? May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends [this work] composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya in the *Svātantryadīpikā*.
The Second Chapter, titled "The Descent of the Supreme Power into the Body," page 80b):

Oṃ. Just as Maheśvara, whose essential nature is the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) between the supreme and the inferior, [projects] all this—which consists of the sense of "this-ness"—by the power of His own Śakti, into the space of His own Self which serves as the foundational ground;
Having effortlessly manifested [the world] and then closed [his eyes], he, being independent, attained oneness with his own nature— which consists of light and bliss— in that very manner; thus,
those who were liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), whose essence was that [nature], remained so from the beginning of saṃsāra until the end of liberation.

Commencing that very illumination which brings delight, he first makes manifest within their hearts the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which has as its nature the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti— their respective natures and limits.
The Great Light, which is manifest, whose nature is supreme bliss, and whose essence is the Great Light—the Divine Consciousness itself—shines forth by means of its own power of self-manifestation;
for manifestation is indeed the nature of being and radiance. That [manifestation]...
Just as light, fire, and darkness— whether external or internal— are perceived as blue, pleasure, and so forth, even though the illumination of the sun and other luminaries,
while manifesting, does not actually convey its own intrinsic nature.

Therefore, for this reason, like the manifestation of blue and other objects, the insentient—having its existence attained through the manifestation of consciousness—is itself self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). [Objection: But why is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*) accepted as being self-luminous?
He says this very thing: because it possesses reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*) is the basis of all things;
through its illumination, all lights and even the suns shine. For the light of consciousness is indeed reflective awareness.
Because it is self-luminous, it is *vimarśa*—that is, its essential nature is the "I-consciousness" (*aham*).
As it has been said: "That which is manifest is not separate from *vimarśa*, and that *vimarśa* is not separate from manifestation; there is no *vimarśa* other than the 'I'."

From the self-nature [of consciousness] arises the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "I am," which is of the single form of consciousness; from this very awareness, everything is produced and attains its existence. For this awareness is the innate, non-artificial nature that constitutes the very self of all things. And so it is said: [Page 83b] From the reflective awareness "I am," which is of the single form of consciousness, everything is produced and has attained its being; for that awareness is the innate, non-artificial nature that is the self of all. Thus, in each case...
In the state of higher knowledge (*abhijñā*), they know the non-dual reflection of the manifestation of all things in their own nature;
for within the Self, the entire universe shines forth. Just as the sprout within the seed contains the manifold arrangement of its future form, so too does consciousness [contain] its own... [p. 84a]
By means of the logic of the essence of reflective awareness (*marśana-sāra-yukti*), [the Lord] grasps the universe as "I am";
for in that way, although light is red, it is not like an insentient object such as crystal.
By virtue of its state of being reflective awareness, this is the primary nature of the Supreme Lord.
Having thoroughly known the Lord— who is one's own self through that very form— as being essentially identical with oneself,
[one realizes] that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that God of gods, whose nature is supreme consciousness, is the Supreme Power (*paramā-śakti*) endowed with all knowledge.

Thus, this power is celebrated as being of the nature of infinite radiance (*anaṃtollāsa*), whose essence is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). It is the power of the supreme speech (*aparavāk*) that reflects upon itself, manifesting in the forms of *paśyantī*,
*madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, and consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

Shining forth by its own nature, it then, through the threefold form of each individual [letter], manifests a ninefold creation of phonemes (*varṇa*) consisting of the play of its own rays, as well as the state (*pada*) consisting of that [creation] and the essential nature of mantra; thus, in the contraction (*pratyāhāra*) of the letters *A* and *Ha*: *pṛ0 85ba)* [End of page 85b]
Because its essential nature consists in the non-differentiation of the Nada and Bindu,

this very [power] has become the tenth energy (vīrya); thus it is said that she alone shines everywhere through the excellence of the principle of consciousness (cittattva), for there is no other means of cognition (pratyaya) in the world.

(86a) That cognition which, even without following after words, is as if permeated by them, is understood through the word; for if the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, it would not shine forth, since it is by that [speech] that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) is possible.
Furthermore, I am the twelve-fold Self and the Swan; Consciousness alone is the Blessed One.
Because it consists of supreme vibration, it is designated as Unmanā.
As the Śruti says, "She creates the worlds," she brings forth all beings from her own nature. Thus, there is a slight [contradiction]... [text ends].

Having attained the state of non-duality consisting of the *lpā* [phonemes], it descends through the sequence beginning with Vyāpinī and ending with the letter *A*, in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is both subtle and gross.
As it has been said: "The eleventh *kala* indeed moves eternally within the *prāṇa*. (p. 87a)

The letter Śa, the letter A, the letter Cu, the letter Ma, and Viṃdu itself; the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Sound (Nāda), and the End of Sound (Nādānta); Śakti and Vyāpinī—Samanā is recorded as the eleventh. Thus it is said.
(p. 87b) [The sequence] from *na* to *tat*, from *tata* to *atīta*, and from *anāmaya*—
extending from the vowel *a* up to the bindu, comprising five measures (*mātrā*) beginning with *nāda* and ending with *vyāpinī*—
these five portions of measures constitute the internal impulse (*ullilasiṣā*) of the Self.

The primary power of the Supreme Lord Haṃsa is Unmanā herself, whose nature is the supreme vibration (*aparaspaṃda*) consisting of the life-force (*aprāṇana*) that serves as the substratum for the non-apprehension of other forms;
she exists in the upward and downward directions, consisting of the radiance of her own rays.

Between the two lotus-like faces, she remains intensely absorbed in love for her own Lord; and for the sake of manifesting the wonder of her own majesty through the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) which are the cause of my composition, she consists of the twelve digits (*kalā*).
Thus, he who has ascended [to that state] possesses an unimpeded nature;
just as the Supreme Lord, by virtue of his own sovereignty, possesses a nature that is everywhere unimpeded, so too does he who has attained identity with Him.
In the operations of the intellect and other faculties, one whose splendor of self-realization has been forgotten becomes,
through the severing of the bonds of identification with the body, of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss;
this is the eternal state consisting of the realization "I am Brahman."

That self-nature belongs to one possessing such a nature; through the penetration (*āveśa*) of the abode of truth (*satyadhāman*), everything becomes immortal. That which consists of the radiance of existence is none other than supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*). Through the penetration of that abode of truth, the entire body, speech, and mind [become immortal].

The nectar of one’s own objective field is the manifestation of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is eternally pervasive and full; thus, the conscious Śiva, whose self is autonomous and pure, shines forth perpetually, as does this supreme power (parā-śakti).

When the resonance of the path of the senses arises within the interior [of consciousness], and its expansion alone throbs as the single essence, this entire world is not born; where would this sound go?
Thus, by the power of that [resonance], the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti) does not descend upon the heart.

(p. 90b) For one who has become upright on the path of pure action, whatever activity proceeds through body, speech, and mind across the three periods of time, that very thing becomes manifest before [him];
moreover, he—udita-...

The yogi is indeed noble; having arisen in nobility, he is ever pure and untainted within the mire of the phenomenal world of māyā—known as the activity of the body, senses, and so forth—just like a lotus in mud. His very nature is one of noble emergence.

Nor is this [consciousness] overwhelmed by the impurities of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), time, limited agency (*kalā*), necessity (*niyati*), passion (*rāga*), and so forth—which are of the nature of the manifestation of its own activity—but rather, it arises from that which is its true essence:
the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) consisting of pure knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, for this [consciousness]...

Knowledge transcends the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and is self-established; it is not dependent on that [organ] as the deluded think, because its nature is the manifest Absolute (*anuttara*). It is the complete fulfillment of the wealth of the manifestation of its own powers, consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).

Such a yogi, whose delusion has been stilled, illuminates them; blessed indeed is he who, having transcended the activity of the three bodies, abides in these three states— that which is called the world, the triple realm, is but a reflection of that [Reality].

Having realized that everything is indeed empty, consisting of the expansion of one's own power, the fortunate one— having attained his goal— remains established in that very self, which is the station of its sovereign lord, whose nature is ultimately immutable, and which is endowed with all sovereignty.

That supreme wisdom sports in the world as its playground; as it is stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "When delusion has been utterly exhausted, when the cloud [of ignorance] has dissolved, when the water-cloud of knowledge has arisen, when reality is fully known, and the Self has been attained... (p. 93a).

The noble one, having investigated what is not desired [by others], perceives that this world is a wandering in the midst of reality, like a reflection seen in a mirror whose form has half dissolved; when the mind is serene, it dwells by force within its own splendor in the heart.
When all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and views have ceased through focused application,
and when the activities of the internal organ proceed toward tranquility before one, then,
with an intellect whose essence is firmly established, the wandering of the world is seen as sporting within Reality (*tattva*).
With a body as expansive as a great chariot, moving with the gait of a horse,
my vital breaths like the reins, and the joy of my movement stirred by the wind, I wander through the world in a form that is both transcendent and immanent.
Having seen this truth through a stainless intellect—that "this world has become such"—one should wander as one who delights in that reality.
Thus, by means of such a nature, [one perceives] within the Self, which is the foundation of all and the support of everything, the entire collection of moving and non-moving beings. (p. 94b)
Knowing that [the Self] abides thus, through the pacification of passion, hatred, pride, and the like,
those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) move about fearlessly in this world; such a knower of reality is the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa) at the station of rest, the manifestation of light.

The repose within the Self is proclaimed as the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva). And that very repose has been described as the cessation of all dependence, and so forth; it is [the state] within one's own self-nature, which is the mass of the light and bliss of consciousness, like a great ocean without waves.
Having come to rest within the Self— the place of repose for vision—
one becomes free from the stain of all doubts concerning bondage and liberation, coming and going, and so forth; at the end, nothing but space remains, for he has become identical with that.
Since the Supreme Lord is of the nature of the consciousness-ether (*cidākāśa*), the support of all space, and the substratum of all things, therefore, even when one has attained identity with Him,
at the time of the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, one remains as if composed of that [consciousness], for His consciousness does not cease.
It does not proceed toward the senses and other categories as previously described;
rather, the indivisible space of consciousness remains even when the jar is destroyed.
This alone is liberation, and not going anywhere else; thus also says the Śruti.

"Of one who has bowed [in devotion], the vital breaths do not depart; they dissolve right there. And being liberated, he reflects"—thus, having analyzed liberation itself according to its different states, it is described as a liberation corresponding to one's own essential nature (*svabhāva*).
By following the gateway of the vision of spontaneous intuition (*pratibhā*) and so forth,

which has become the very life-force of those respective designations and expressions, there occurs an ascent to the state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*)— which is stainless— and the blossoming of the sovereignty of the nature of the Fourth (*turya*).
Liberation is of such a nature as it takes on the corresponding essential nature [of its cause], just as when Prakṛti has mounted the state of a Puruṣa, she becomes independent;
and once bound souls have ascended to the station of a Siddha, they maintain their physical body (piṇḍa) according to their will. (p. 97b)

Having joined the five elements— which have become their own self in the form of consciousness, completely filled with the perfection of all sovereignty— into the five elements, they shine brilliantly as the nature of the unobscured sky of consciousness.

Just as Śukadeva and others, having ascended to the state of Īśvara, being independent great Māyās whose bodies are the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), fashion the arrangement of bodies or bodilessness according to their own will by the power of their own *śakti*. Just so...

Hari, Hara, and others— having shed the conceit of bodily identity, being indifferent toward *māyā-prakṛti*, and resting in the nectar of bliss— abandon their bodies composed of the five elements right here at the final moment, merging into the Supreme like milk into milk.
They become merged in the void; thus, within this fourfold manner of liberation, there are infinite varieties according to the gradations of intensity.

Here too, as in the case of those endowed with the status of a lord of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) and so forth, when the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (*parameśvara-śaktipāta*) occurs—*pṛ0 99a*.

"Thus [ends] the auspicious Nibandhana. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Liberation while Living," in the *Svātantryadīpikā* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Māheśvara school. 3.

All days are indeed the measurers [of time],
for by the Śruti text, "Verily, these beings are born from Ānanda," Ānanda is the nourisher everywhere;
shining with supreme excellence, it is that which is desired even by Brahmā and the other gods.

[The sequence consists of: "I give," the internal surging [of intention], the accomplishment [of the act], memory, the removal [of obstacles], pride, determination, volition, the vital breaths, internal discourse,
the manifestation of those respective sounds, the intellect, the sense organs, and the action organs— each of these [constituting] the respective [stages].

(p. 101a) Among those infinite powers whose essential nature is vibration, I am the Lord, the leader, whose own nature is self-luminous and who serves as the distinct substratum; I abide perfectly, even while active through their various manifestations.
Even while performing [these activities], one remains established in the state of the Great Hero (mahāvīrya), which is the nature of the imperishable;

for there is no change in my own nature of imperishable bliss (*acyutānanda*) due to the differences between those various states. Indeed, these [states] enter as the qualities of their respective functions.
Just as the various currents of rivers do not cause the ocean— which is by nature free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*)— to become wavy, so too, while abiding in its own essential nature,
the Great [Lord] has ascended to the state of the Lord of that power and remains with his luminous form undiminished.
The Hero, by means of his power of supreme illumination, demonstrates that he illuminates all of this;

it is the manifestation of his own power, the Supreme Power whose essence is the reflective awareness of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), thinking "I am," which is his very nature, occurring simultaneously.

(p. 102b) Because it possesses the nature of opening and closing its eyes, [the Lord], having by his own will manifested from his own essential nature— which serves as the foundational wall— the multitude of those respective infinite powers,
[establishes them] within the Great Void that is his self-luminous nature, consisting of their very vibration.
It shines intensely within its own self;

its rays are the various functions existing in those respective locations, which are designated as various powers (*śakti*). There is nothing else whatsoever apart from that, for she is inherently devoid of action and is the essence of those various [powers].

I alone am independent, for through the play of my own nature, I have withdrawn from all engagement with those various activities; by resting in me, who am the very essence of all vital breath (*prāṇana*), those intent on serving me have become free from the operations of opening and closing the eyes.

In these two states of burning (*dāha-avasthā*), the Hero, having withdrawn all functions and powers, flows as a single convergence without outward expansion; he whose nature is dissolved in each respective station is that which is the internal and external opening and closing of the eyes (*nimeṣonmeṣa*).

On page 104a): In this independent [work], I myself am Śiva; by the power of my own sovereignty, having become Śiva and Īśvara, I bring about at will those two states consisting of closing and opening for them, for there is nothing apart from me.
Because there is something [which is] the truth according to my own view:

the supreme power of consciousness (*aparā-saṃvit*), whose nature is the manifestation and bliss of "I," which consists of the self-reflection of the "I," and whose essence is the radiance of the existence that constitutes my very own nature.

Whatever exists— whether external or internal— that has been manifested, all that is indeed covered by me alone, the Lord of Consciousness, who has attained true being through the majestic power of the light of innate consciousness, from Brahmā down to a mere ant.

Having manifested this universe—consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—within the sky of my own Self which serves as its foundation, I manifest as the designation and expression of their respective natures; thus it is said: "The one who is the sole locus of designations."

There is no otherness of this Self due to the difference in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I" and so forth; for, according to the principle that "this [Self] is perceived precisely as the substrate of the notion 'I'," it remains one even within the manifold variety of the universe— which consists of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge— across its various states.

I alone am the supreme subject, whose nature consists of the vitalizing breath (anuprāṇana); I, being autonomous and pure, freely dance as the supreme actor within those various states, yet there is no alteration of my own essential nature in those conditions, because my sole nature is the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃpratyavamarśa).
The notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is by nature unimpeded everywhere and is the impeller everywhere;
this very point he clarifies: "All that begins with my command is the majestic power of my own essence (*vasuśakti*)," having expanded it appropriately everywhere. Tri... [p. 106b]

I am the sovereign emperor over the three worlds; indeed, no one anywhere ever engages in their own activity without my impulsion. It is I alone who, through my own power in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in all beings, [reside] in those various places and those various bodies.

Having become the very nature of [all] things, I perform those various activities consisting of successive stages according to my will; yet, in those various states and activities, there is no agitation whatsoever in my own autonomous and ever-unwavering self-nature, which consists of supreme bliss.

107b) Because [I] possess the nature of both the pervaded and the pervader within those various teachings, my body is completely filled with the essence of the contemplative realization (*parāmarśa*) of the wonder and marvel of the expansion of my own sovereign power (*nija-vibhūti*). Gaṃ.
Frightened and agitated by his own nature, he is satisfied only with himself; thus,
because all stains of agitation have fallen away, his nature is eternally risen, consisting of pure consciousness and bliss, transcending the universe even while being identical with the universe.
My own essential nature shines forth with supreme excellence; therefore, my form is free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), devoid of enemies, friends, home, wife,
heaven, hell, liberation, transformation, human beings, power, or even Śiva.
The conceptualization of the individual soul (ka), the vital breath (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara), as well as Brahmā, is of the nature of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
That which is devoid of these adjuncts is the pure, stainless Great Space (mahākāśa), my own form.
I alone am that which consists of the self-reflection of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa), whose essential nature is supreme bliss-consciousness (paramānanda-saṃvit-svabhāva). I am indeed the Nirvāṇa.

Because my nature transcends all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like the fierce sun, and because I abide in the state of supreme peace, I experience the wonder of play that is both immanent in the universe and transcendent of it;
therefore, I am Śiva, the self-dependent Great Space. I am indeed... [the rest of the sentence continues].
The Lord, who is the supreme mass of bliss and pure consciousness, though consisting of the universe, is transcendent of the universe;

and though transcendent of the universe, his essential nature consists of the universe. He performs a play, which is the expansion of His own power, whose nature is both sequential and non-sequential.

Having fashioned [the world] according to his own will within his very self— the pure supreme space consisting of the expansion of his own radiance— he shines forth by the excellence of his own sovereignty; shining as the independent Self, he is resplendent with beautiful [forms] both external and internal.

(p. 110a) With the essence of the internal cavity of the *kṣīvit* sound, I am Bhairava, the Great Bliss, greedy for the stainless activity at the seat of power (*śaktipīṭha*), [thinking] "I am Śiva"—thus [ends] the auspicious [work].
Thus [ends] the work composed by the most excellent teacher of the venerable Mahāmāheśvara school...
